semantic_correction.stem: Which parent statement shows correct understanding of early hunger cues in a healthy full-term infant?

options.A: I will watch for rooting, hand-to-mouth movements, lip smacking, or increased alertness and offer a feeding before the baby reaches vigorous crying.
options.B: I will wait until the baby cries strongly before offering a feeding because crying is the earliest and most reliable sign that the baby is hungry.
options.C: I will use a fixed clock schedule and delay feeding when hunger cues appear early, because cue-based feeding can make the baby's intake unpredictable.
options.D: I will treat every episode of hand sucking or mouthing as hunger and offer another feeding even when the baby has recently eaten and shows no other cues.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current American Academy of Pediatrics guidance supports responsive feeding and advises caregivers to respond to early hunger cues rather than waiting for crying. AAP examples of early cues include rooting, hand-to-mouth behavior, lip smacking or licking, increased alertness, and suckling motions; crying is described as a late sign of hunger. Current CDC materials independently list putting hands to the mouth, turning the head toward the breast or bottle, and smacking or licking the lips as hunger signs. These cues should be interpreted in context because some sucking or hand-to-mouth behavior can also be self-soothing rather than hunger. Therefore the parent should look for a pattern of early hunger cues and feed responsively before vigorous crying develops. B is incorrect because crying is a late rather than early hunger sign. C is incorrect because responsive feeding uses infant cues rather than rigidly ignoring hunger signals until a scheduled time. D is incorrect because a single nonspecific behavior such as sucking does not always indicate hunger.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Teach caregivers to recognize and respond to early infant hunger cues such as rooting, hand-to-mouth behavior, lip smacking, and increased alertness rather than waiting for crying or relying on rigid schedules.

semantic_correction.source_locator: AAP How Often To Breastfeed: crying is a late hunger sign; earlier cues include lip smacking, suckling motions, rooting, movement, and increased alertness. AAP Responsive Feeding Explained: caregivers should recognize and respond to hunger and fullness cues. CDC infant guidance: hunger signs include hands to mouth, turning toward breast or bottle, and smacking or licking lips; CDC 2026 mPINC defines cue-based/on-demand feeding as feeding in response to hunger cues rather than a fixed schedule.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Current AAP and CDC guidance directly supports responsive feeding based on early hunger cues, identifies rooting/hand-to-mouth/lip behaviors as hunger signs, and states that crying is a late hunger cue rather than the preferred trigger to begin feeding.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed absolute-word and answer-length cues, rebuilt all four parent statements to comparable length and specificity, freshly verified current AAP and CDC feeding-cue guidance, and preserved recognition of early hunger cues before crying as the single best response.

audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests early infant hunger-cue recognition with one clearly best response, balanced alternatives, current authoritative guidance, and no absolute-word or length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It identifies established early hunger cues and appropriately responds before late-stage crying.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. AAP guidance describes crying as a late hunger sign rather than the earliest or preferred trigger for feeding.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Responsive feeding relies on hunger and fullness cues rather than ignoring clear hunger cues until a rigid clock time.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Sucking and mouthing can occur for reasons other than hunger and should be interpreted with the infant's overall cue pattern and recent feeding context.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A uniquely reflects responsive feeding and established early hunger cues; B waits for a late cue, C ignores cues for a rigid schedule, and D overinterprets a nonspecific behavior.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel parent statements of comparable length and specificity; prior absolute-word distractors and the uniquely-long correct response were removed.
